strengths: Novel and well-motivated contribution: the paper provides the first mechanistic (SAE-based) analysis of unexpected code-switching in LLMs, connecting the phenomenon to abnormally high pre-activation values of language-specific features, which goes beyond prior heuristic solutions (e.g., GRPO with language consistency rewards).

The proposed SASFT method is technically sound and practical: it internalizes the finding into an auxiliary loss during SFT rather than requiring inference-time intervention, making it deployable without extra inference overhead.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: five models across three model families, three target languages, two data scales, comparison against two baselines (SFT, SFT+GRPO), six multilingual benchmarks showing capabilities are preserved or improved, plus in-depth analyses (layer selection, feature selection) and an ablation on the threshold choice (SASFT_zero).
Good scientific rigor: statistical significance testing (two-proportion Z-tests) is provided, and limitations are candidly discussed in Appendix F.

The feasibility study (Figures 3-4) establishes a causal link between language-feature pre-activation and code-switching through directional ablation, giving the method a solid mechanistic foundation.
weaknesses: Reproducibility concerns: the SFT training data is proprietary and the code is not released, which limits the ability of others to verify or build upon the core results.

Limited generality of the analysis and method: only three target languages (Chinese, Russian, Korean) are studied, all with unique scripts, making code-switching detection trivial via GlotScript; the paper does not address harder cases (Latin-script language pairs) or how the method generalizes when the 'unexpected' language is not known in advance or when SAEs of sufficient quality are unavailable.

The method depends on prior knowledge of which language causes code-switching (language-specific features must be identified per language per model), and requires training or obtaining SAEs; this limits applicability to practical scenarios where the problematic language set is unknown or broader.

Baseline coverage is thin: only SFT and SFT+GRPO are compared. Other natural baselines, such as inference-time feature ablation/steering (the paper's own Section 3.2 method), data-augmentation or language-consistency approaches, and the SASFT_Enhance variant in the main comparison, are not included in the main results.

Some experimental choices are only partially justified: the main results use 'last two layers and first two features' with λ=0.05 selected via grid search, raising concerns about tuning on evaluation data; several reported reductions (e.g., Gemma-2-9B cases) are small or not statistically significant, and the paper's strong claims (e.g., 'consistently reduces by more than 50%') slightly overstate the uniformity of results.

The model scale is limited (all models under 9B) and experiments use base models fine-tuned on the authors' private instruction data, so it is unclear whether SASFT would fix code-switching in already-deployed instruct models (e.g., DeepSeek-R1 itself) without full re-finetuning.

The code-switching ratio magnitudes are very small for some models (e.g., 0.2-0.3%), making some reductions of limited practical significance, and the 'distance' constraint in Eq. (1) is operationalized only loosely via benchmark performance.

strengths: The paper addresses a practical, under-explored problem (unexpected code-switching in multilingual LLMs) with a mechanistic angle: using sparse autoencoders to show that code-switching correlates with unusually high pre-activation values of target-language features, and validating this with directional ablation experiments (Figures 3 and 4).

The proposed SASFT method is a reasonable translation of the mechanistic finding into a training-time intervention, and the paper demonstrates that inference-time ablation alone is insufficient, motivating the approach.

Evaluation is relatively broad: five models across three families, three target languages, two dataset scales, and six multilingual benchmarks, with statistical significance testing (Appendix E) and several ablations (layer selection, feature selection, threshold setting α_j, an 'enhance' variant in Appendix C).
The paper is generally well written and organized, with a clear problem formulation (Section 2) and honest discussion of limitations in Appendix F.
weaknesses: A potentially serious evaluation flaw: code-switching detection relies solely on Unicode script ranges (GlotScript), flagging any Han characters as Chinese. Since the evaluation data includes Japanese queries (Appendix B), and Japanese text contains Kanji (Han script), Japanese responses would be falsely counted as code-switching to Chinese. This could inflate baselines and confound the reported ratios; the paper does not address this confound or report per-source-language results for the main tables.

Limited baseline coverage: the only comparisons are standard SFT and SFT+GRPO. Simpler and natural baselines are missing, e.g., data curation for language consistency during SFT, decoding-time language constraints, or steering-vector interventions adapted to training. Given the modest absolute CS ratios (often <2%, sometimes <0.5%), the practical significance of reductions is hard to judge without these comparisons.

Signs of possible test-set leakage in hyperparameter selection: λ is chosen by grid search (0.01–2, step 0.01) and layer/feature choices ('last two layers, first two features') are fixed for main results, but it is unclear what data these choices were tuned on; if tuned on the evaluation set, the reported gains may be optimistic.

Some results are inconsistent with the narrative and not adequately explained, e.g., SASFT reduces CS by only 7% for Gemma-2-9B (230k, zh), the abstract's 'more than 50% in most cases' vs. '26 of 30' phrasing, and the suspicious +17.7 HumanEval gain for Llama-3.1-8B that goes unexplained.

Reproducibility is weak: training data is proprietary and code is not released ('plan to release after internal review'), and for Qwen3 models the paper trains its own SAEs with insufficient detail on their quality/configurations, which materially affects feature identification.

Novelty is incremental: the core building blocks (language-specific SAE features, the monolinguality metric, directional ablation) come directly from Deng et al. [5]; the contribution is mainly applying these to code-switching with a ReLU-threshold auxiliary loss, which is a fairly standard regularization construction.

Generalization is narrow: only three target languages with distinct scripts, all models under 9B, and the analysis is correlational in parts (the causal link between feature pre-activation and code-switching is supported only by ablation at a single token position).

strengths: Novel and well-motivated angle: the paper connects unexpected code-switching in LLMs to pre-activation values of language-specific SAE features, providing the first mechanistic (interpretability-based) analysis of this practical, user-facing problem rather than treating it as a black-box RL issue.

The feasibility study is convincing: Figure 3 shows pre-activation values rise before the switch point, and Figure 4 demonstrates causal evidence via directional ablation (ablating the Chinese feature reduces switching while ablating English features does not), which supports the central hypothesis rather than leaving it purely correlational.

SASFT is a simple, well-integrated method: the auxiliary loss (Eq. 8) directly operationalizes the mechanistic finding, avoids inference-time intervention, and the design choice of pre-estimated thresholds (vs. zero) is validated in the ablation (Table 3).

Broad empirical evaluation: five models across three families, two dataset scales, three target languages, six multilingual benchmarks, with statistical significance testing (Appendix E) that goes beyond typical practice for this type of work.

Consistent and substantial results: >50% reduction in 26/30 cases with several complete eliminations, while benchmark performance is largely preserved or improved, addressing the key concern that suppressing language features could damage multilingual capability.

In-depth analysis of layers and features (Figures 6-7) provides useful practical guidance (multi-layer/multi-feature is more stable) and shows the authors probed the method rather than just reporting headline numbers.
weaknesses: Limited language scope: the method and evaluation only cover Chinese, Russian, and Korean, and detection relies on script distinctiveness (Han/Cyrillic/Hangul). Extending to languages sharing scripts (e.g., European languages mixing with English) is non-trivial and unaddressed, limiting generality.

The mechanistic claim, while supported, is established only through correlational statistics plus ablation at the final layer; a more rigorous causal analysis (e.g., patching at multiple positions/layers, or showing the reverse - artificially high pre-activations induce switching) would strengthen the story.

Baselines are thin: the only competitive comparison is SFT+GRPO with a language-consistency reward. Simple alternatives such as constraining decoding to target-language tokens, language-specific logit biasing, or instruction-level prompt mitigation are not compared, making it hard to judge the cost-benefit of SAE-guided training.

Some improvements lack statistical significance (e.g., Gemma-2-9B zh/ru entries in Table 5, and SASFT's -7% on Gemma-2-9B zh in Table 1), so the claim of 'consistently' reducing code-switching by >50% overstates the evidence in a few configurations.

Training data is proprietary and code is not released ('after internal team review'), which limits reproducibility of a method that depends on careful reproduction of the SFT setup; also, the datasets are artificially composed (deliberately imbalanced language mixtures), so the severity of code-switching in realistic deployment settings (e.g., the 37% baseline for Qwen3-1.7B) may be overstated.

Method depends on external SAEs (Gemma Scope, Llama Scope) or training custom SAEs, adding pipeline complexity; the paper does not discuss how sensitive results are to SAE quality or how the approach applies to models without available SAEs.
All models are under 9B; no evidence the approach scales to frontier-size models where code-switching is also reported.

strengths: Novel and practically relevant problem framing: the paper formalizes 'Code-Switching Reduction in LLMs' as a task and provides, to the authors' knowledge, the first mechanistic analysis of unexpected code-switching using sparse autoencoders.

The analysis (Section 3) is well executed: it shows a clear pre-activation pattern of the target-language feature preceding code-switch events (Fig. 3), demonstrates suppression via directional ablation (Fig. 4), and, importantly, provides bidirectional causal evidence in Appendix K by showing feature enhancement induces code-switching. This goes beyond mere correlation and gives the method a solid mechanistic grounding.
SASFT is a simple, principled method directly derived from the analysis (penalizing pre-activation of target-language features during SFT), requiring no inference-time overhead.

Comprehensive evaluation: 5 models across 3 families, 3 target languages, 2 dataset scales, with consistent reductions (>50% in 23/30 cases), outperforming GRPO and SFT+Penalty baselines, plus capability preservation checks on 6-7 benchmarks and ablations on layer/feature selection and threshold setting (SASFTzero).

Good reproducibility posture: implementation details, hyperparameters, dataset statistics, and code/data release are provided; robustness of language-feature identification across SAE configurations is verified in Appendix J; limitations and LLM usage are honestly stated.
weaknesses: Limited language scope: the script-based detection approach restricts the study to Chinese, Russian, and Korean (distinct scripts). The method and evaluation cannot be assessed for the arguably harder and more common case of Latin-script language mixing (e.g., English<->French/Spanish), limiting generalization claims.
Model scale is modest (all models <9B); the abstract claims broad multilingual impact, but effectiveness on larger instruction-tuned production models is untested.

Practical significance of some results is questionable: baseline code-switching ratios are often below 1%, and in several cases the absolute reduction (e.g., 0.78->0.41) is small; the paper could better quantify real-world impact or report statistical significance/variance over runs.

The mechanistic analysis builds heavily on Deng et al. (2025) (feature identification metric, language-specific features), making the analysis contribution somewhat incremental; concurrent work (Wang et al., 2025a; Nie et al., 2025) also relates language mixing to internal representations, so the 'first in-depth analysis' claim could be softened.

Hyperparameter sensitivity of the auxiliary loss weight lambda is not reported (only grid-search ranges); also the SFT+Penalty baseline is self-proposed, so the strongest comparison is a method designed by the authors, and GRPO's instability may partly reflect tuning limitations rather than the paradigm.
Minor presentation issues: broken URL in the abstract, typos (e.g., 'Chinsese' in Appendix K), and a somewhat cluttered evaluation narrative (six vs. seven benchmarks listed inconsistently).

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant and under-explored problem (unexpected code-switching in multilingual LLMs) and frames a clear task definition with an evaluation metric (code-switching ratio).

The mechanistic analysis is reasonably thorough: it goes beyond correlation by providing both ablation (Section 3.3.2) and enhancement (Appendix K) experiments, offering bidirectional causal evidence linking language-specific SAE feature pre-activations to code-switching.

The proposed SASFT method is simple, well-motivated by the analysis, and evaluated at unusual breadth for this kind of interpretability-guided intervention: 5 models from 3 families, 3 target languages, 2 dataset scales, 6 benchmarks, plus ablations over layers, features, and threshold settings (SASFT_zero) and an SAE-hyperparameter robustness study (Appendix J).
Results are generally consistent: SASFT reduces code-switching in most settings (often >50%) while largely preserving benchmark performance, and code/data availability supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core ingredients (language-specific SAE features, their monolinguality metric, and directional ablation) are all taken from Deng et al. (2025). The contribution reduces to adding a ReLU-based auxiliary penalty on pre-activations during SFT, which is an incremental application rather than a new technique.

Positioning is overstated: the paper claims to provide 'the first in-depth analysis' of unexpected code-switching, yet related work (Wang et al., 2025a; Nie et al., 2025) already studies internal causes of language mixing/language confusion; the related-work section does not clearly differentiate the contribution.

Weak and incomplete baselines: only SFT, SFT+GRPO, and SFT+Penalty are compared. Missing obvious alternatives include inference-time feature steering (which the authors themselves show works in Section 3.3.2), DPO with language-consistency preferences, decoding-time constraints, and prompt-based mitigation. GRPO's instability (+157% in one case) may reflect weak tuning rather than a fundamental limitation, weakening the 'SASFT significantly outperforms existing methods' claim.

Narrow scope of languages: evaluation is restricted to Chinese, Russian, and Korean explicitly because these scripts are trivially detectable via Unicode ranges. This is a significant limitation — Latin-script language mixing (e.g., English-French/Spanish), arguably a common real-world case, cannot be evaluated with the proposed detection method, limiting the generality of both the analysis and the solution.

Evaluation concerns: no statistical significance testing, variance over seeds, or confidence intervals are reported, yet many relative improvements are computed on very small base rates (e.g., 0.05% → 0.01% reported as -79%), where a handful of generations can swing the numbers. Absolute code-switching ratios are low (~0.2-1%) in many settings, raising questions about practical significance.

Inconsistency between feasibility study and main experiments: the feasibility analysis (Figure 2) uses instruct models, while main experiments use base models; results on one may not transfer to the other. Also, several benchmark drops are non-trivial (e.g., Qwen3-8B HellaSwag -2.88, Gemma-2-9B Flores -1.18), and the claim of 'maintains or even improves' performance is stronger than the evidence in the worst cases.

The formal objective in Eq. (1) with Dist(L, L*) is loosely operationalized (performance difference on benchmarks), and hyperparameters (λ, layer/feature selection) are grid-searched per model, making the reported comparisons somewhat optimistic without held-out validation details.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated task formulation: the paper clearly defines Code-Switching Reduction with a formal objective (Eq. 1) and a measurable metric (Eq. 2), addressing a real, user-facing problem in multilingual LLMs that prior work (Guo et al., 2025) touched only superficially.

Strong mechanistic analysis: the paper goes beyond treating code-switching as a black-box problem by showing (1) pre-activation values of target-language features rise before a switch occurs (Fig. 3), (2) directional ablation of the target-language feature reduces code-switching (Fig. 4), and (3) directional enhancement induces code-switching (Appendix K). This bidirectional causal evidence substantially strengthens the central hypothesis.

The proposed method (SASFT) is a principled translation of the mechanistic finding into a training-time auxiliary loss (Eq. 8), avoiding inference-time intervention overhead — a sensible and well-argued design choice.

Comprehensive evaluation: five models across three model families, three target languages, two dataset scales, and six multilingual benchmarks; SASFT consistently beats SFT, SFT+GRPO, and SFT+Penalty baselines with >50% reductions in most settings while maintaining or improving benchmark performance.

Good ablation coverage: layer selection (Fig. 6), feature selection (Fig. 7), threshold choice α_j (Table 3), the enhance-vs-reduce variant (Appendix F), and robustness of language features across SAE hyperparameters (Appendix J) all support the method's design decisions.
Reproducibility appears reasonable: datasets, hyperparameters, training times, and detection methodology are documented, and code/data are stated to be released.
weaknesses: Limited practical significance of absolute numbers: code-switching ratios are quite low even for the SFT baseline (often 0.1–3.5%), so the large relative reductions (which drive the headline claims) correspond to small absolute differences. The paper should discuss whether these differences are practically meaningful and report statistical significance or variance across runs/seeds.

Potential evaluation–training overlap: the training corpora include Flores and GSM8KInstruct data, while Flores (and pmmeval-sourced benchmarks) are also used for evaluation and for the code-switching evaluation set. This contamination risk is not addressed or controlled for.

Weak baseline tuning: SFT+GRPO performs erratically (e.g., +157% for Llama-3.1-8B on Korean), suggesting possible under-tuning rather than inherent inferiority; additionally, the inference-time steering approach validated in Section 3.3.2 is not included as a baseline, even though it directly addresses the same problem.

Scope restricted to script-distinct target languages (Chinese, Russian, Korean) because detection relies on Unicode script ranges (Appendix E.3); the method's applicability to Latin-script targets (e.g., French, Spanish) is untested, which limits generality of the task definition and the method.

Per-model hyperparameter selection (λ, learning rate, layers, features) appears to be tuned against the same evaluation data used for reporting, raising concerns about test-set overfitting; a held-out selection protocol would strengthen the claims.
All models are ≤9B and only SFT-time constraints are explored; scaling behavior and integration with preference-based tuning (DPO/GRPO) are left to future work, as acknowledged in Appendix G.

Minor presentation issues: the symbol λ is used for both the ablation coefficient (Eq. 6) and the loss weight (Eq. 9); Table 2 reports only the Chinese 110k setting in the main text; some citation errors (e.g., Qwen-3 report cited as Yang et al. 2025 with wrong title, "MGSM (Shi et al., 2022)" vs 2023); Eq. 8 notation for the expectation over datasets is slightly loose.
